qt: to the Commission Carles Puigdemont i Casamajó (NI), Antoni Comín i Oliveres (NI) Subject:

Citrus production in Catalonia follows EU phytosanitary norms that are not always followed by producers in non-EU countries. The EU’s Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed has revealed that, since the beginning of 2024, batches of citrus fruits from Türkiye1 and from Egypt have been rejected due to the excessive presence of pesticides banned in the EU2. Moreover, working conditions in these countries are poor, with salaries of between EUR 5 and EUR 10 per day3. Catalonia’s citrus farmers’ pay will fall by between 60 % and 80 % this season compared to last season: oranges account for a third of citrus production, and clementine-type tangerines the other two thirds. Of these, a harvest of about 88 500 tonnes is expected, a significant drop since 2021, when 130 000 tonnes were harvested. Finally, Catalonia’s citrus farmers are mostly smallholders or SMEs4. Valencian farmers are experiencing similar problems5. 1.
Will the Commission introduce the antidumping procedure set in place by Regulation (EU) 2016/10366and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17937to help Catalan citrus farmers?
How will the Commission ensure that Catalan and European citrus producers will not incur excessive financial losses due to the abovementioned facts?
at: (English version) to the Commission Carles Puigdemont i Casamajó (NI), Antoni Comín i Oliveres (NI) (15 February 2024) Subject: Unfair competition due to dumping in the Catalan and Valencian citrus fruit sector Citrus production in Catalonia follows EU phytosanitary norms that are not always followed by producers in non-EU countries. The EU’s Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed has revealed that, since the beginning of 2024, batches of citrus fruits from Türkiye (1) and from Egypt have been rejected due to the excessive presence of pesticides banned in the EU (2). Moreover, working conditions in these countries are poor, with salaries of between EUR 5 and EUR 10 per day (3). Catalonia’s citrus farmers’ pay will fall by between 60% and 80% this season compared to last season: oranges account for a third of citrus production, and clementine-type tangerines the other two thirds. Of these, a harvest of about 88 500 tonnes is expected, a significant drop since 2021, when 130 000 tonnes were harvested. Finally, Catalonia’s citrus farmers are mostly smallholders or SMEs (4). Valencian farmers are experiencing similar problems (5). 1. Will the Commission introduce the antidumping procedure set in place by Regulation (EU) 2016/1036 (6)and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1793 (7)to help Catalan citrus farmers? 2. How will the Commission ensure that Catalan and European citrus producers will not incur excessive financial losses due to the above-mentioned facts? (30 April 2024) The Commission is committed to protect any EU industry from unfair and injurious trading practices by robustly using the trade defence instruments. The Commission can open an investigation regarding imports of any product, if it receives a complaint from industry in accordance with the basic anti-dumping Regulation (8). Citrus producers exposed to unfair and injurious trading practices should contact the Directorate General for Trade (9). Citrus fruits from Türkiye and Egypt are subject to increased official controls when entering the EU at harmonised frequencies (10), in view of their potential contamination with pesticide residues. Oranges from Türkiye need to be sampled, tested and certified by the competent authorities prior to their export to the EU. These measures are periodically reviewed. The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) contributes to the resilience of farms by providing decoupled income support to stabilise income. In addition, support exists for producer organisations with sectoral interventions and for green investments or farming practices helping climate adaptation. These apply also to the citrus sector. Under the CAP Strategic plans, members of a producer organisation may benefit from mutual funds if implemented under an operational programme. Any loss of turn-over of the producer organisation may also be compensated via the method to be applied for the calculation of the value of marketed production in such circumstances.

This avoids any negative impact on the implementation of the operational programme. Moreover, the exceptional market measures adopted by the Commission in 2022 and 2023 were used by Spanish Government, respectively, to support the citrus sector and the fruit sector affected by drought, notably in Catalonia.
